rows.verified: Health surveillance uses repeated health checks to identify ill health caused by work.
Health surveillance is required when workers remain exposed to relevant health risks after controls are in place.
Noise, vibration and hazardous substances are examples of risks that can require health surveillance.
Schemes should usually be established with input from a competent occupational-health professional.
Certain hazards, including asbestos, lead and ionising radiation, can require medical surveillance.
Where appointed-doctor medical surveillance is required, the employer must use an HSE-appointed occupational-health doctor, subject to stated exceptions.
Health surveillance is distinct from general health screening, health promotion and health monitoring.
Results provide feedback on controls, allow workers to raise concerns and support further prevention and training.
Health-surveillance value depends on the hazard, exposure, test validity, frequency, worker participation, clinical competence and follow-up action.
HSE surveillance evidence is worker-, hazard-, exposure-, test-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level illness probability.
Workplaces need plans for emergencies that may have wider impacts.
Special procedures may be needed for serious injury, explosion, flood, poisoning, electrocution, fire, radioactive release and chemical spills.
Reliable emergency response is supported by competent trained people and regular realistic practice.
Plans, actions and responsibilities should be clearly agreed, recorded and rehearsed.
Emergency plans should explain how alarms are raised and how emergency services are contacted.
Escape routes, emergency exits and emergency lighting must be suitable, available and kept unobstructed.
Competent people should be nominated to take control and key isolation or shutdown actions should be defined.
Work should not resume while serious danger remains.
Emergency response depends on event type, occupancy, layout, communications, staffing, vulnerable people, equipment and external-service access.
HSE emergency guidance is site-, incident-, workforce-, communication-, equipment- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level casualty probability.
The responsible person must carry out and keep up to date a construction-site fire risk assessment.
The responsible person is usually the main or principal contractor controlling the site.
Fire precautions should be based on identified fuel and ignition sources.
The risk assessment should address means of escape.
The site needs a suitable means of giving warning in the event of fire.
The site needs appropriate means of fighting fire based on the assessed risk.
Work in occupied buildings must not compromise existing escape routes, fire separation, alarms, dry risers or sprinkler systems.
Timber-frame and other higher-risk construction may require significant additional precautions.
Construction-fire risk depends on project phase, materials, temporary works, ignition sources, occupancy, compartmentation, access and emergency controls.
HSE construction-fire guidance is project-, phase-, material-, occupancy-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level fire probability.
